claims.text: The target material is a defect-free, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy.
Experimental HfNbTaTiZr variants contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed framework will compute lattice and electronic thermal conductivity separately.
Machine-learned force fields combined with Green–Kubo calculations can capture the effects of atomic-scale static and dynamic distortions on lattice heat transport.
DFT-based Boltzmann transport can independently evaluate electron-scattering processes in HfNbTaTiZr.
Local lattice distortions arise from atomic-size mismatch and non-ideal atomic positions in disordered alloys.
Static and dynamic lattice distortions modulate phonon scattering.
Lattice distortion and nanostructural complexity alter electronic characteristics in high-entropy alloys.
Independently treating phonon and electron scattering avoids conflation associated with average Debye-temperature or perfect-crystal approximations.
Earlier HfNbTaTiZr models based on Debye temperatures and averaged defect-free crystals conflate or misestimate lattice and electronic contributions.
Earlier predictive methods have uncertainties as large as ±30%.
Above 300 K, the proposed method will predict lattice thermal conductivity 20–30% below the values from previous models.
The 20–30% reduction will constitute an improvement in predictive accuracy.
For oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr between 300 and 1200 K, the relevant measured total thermal conductivity is 10–17 W/(K m).
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr are of comparable magnitude.

In the cited NiCoFeCrMn and NiCoFeCrPd concentrated alloys, lattice thermal conductivity dominates at low temperature and becomes comparable to electronic thermal conductivity around room temperature.
Chemical disorder in concentrated alloys can scatter electrons more effectively than phonons.
The temperature dependence of lattice thermal conductivity in disordered alloys is theoretically difficult to describe.
The proposed model may deviate for alloys with additional phases, high defect densities, or stronger electron–phonon interactions than it treats.

The hypothesis is falsified if predicted lattice conductivity differs from measurement by more than ±10% above 300 K, if the two contributions are not comparable below 200 K, or if oxygen-containing samples do not exhibit total conductivity within 10–17 W/(K m).

contradictions.description: The initial state is called defect-free while also including variants with 1 wt.% oxygen; oxygen impurities are incompatible with an unqualified defect-free description unless the two sample classes are explicitly separated.

A 20–30% reduction in predicted lattice conductivity is treated as equivalent to a 20–30% improvement in predictive accuracy, although a change in the predicted value and a reduction in prediction error are different quantities.
